- I appreciate your interest in this issue and realize it may take time to evaluate. There may well be other and better ways to address this issue. I took a minimalist approach which I hoped would reduce the chance of actually making things worse. I briefly considered a more aggressive approach. My thought was to make each thread have its own main loop (and get rid of ThreadJob) and permanently assign each thread one or more partitions to work with. Basically simulate the individual JVM approach with threads. Each thread would round robin among the assigned partitions, but, there would be no notion of fairness between threads. The JVM would do the load sharing between threads much as the OS controlled load sharing between multiple JVMs (each with there own set of partitions) for the single threaded approach. I also considered relaxing the notion of fairness between threads by keeping the Chooser full (calling tryUpdate as soon as the previous message was inserted). Both those ideas sounded more like features than bug fixes and would require extensive design, review, and testing. I therefore did not pursue them, but, it would not surprise me if you suggested something equally different from what I have coded up.
- Sorry that it took so long. Thanks a lot for this patch. As you already analyzed very thoroughly, this is a flaw in current AsyncRunLoop that relies on the poll timeout to avoid busy loop, which caused long delays for tasks which have already completed processing. The way of your fix makes sense to me: AsyncRunLoop should use the latch to wait instead of relying on poll timeout.This will allow the other tasks to proceed. Nice work! For the fix implementation, I notice two things: 1) Did you also configure task.poll.interval.ms to be 0 in order to get rid of the poll waiting? Seems to me it's a must since otherwise the run loop will still poll quite often in case of empty partitions. To this point, looks like we don't need the poll timeout (task.poll.inverval.ms) anymore after this change, since runloop will control the poll interval, and we should immediately return after systemconsumers.poll() in any case. If this is the case, would you mind also make SystemConsumers.poll() always return without waiting? 2) seems the logic of blockIfNoWork() can be moved into blockIfBusy(), basically doing the same check of null envelope and wait if no worker is available. Is that something feasible? Thanks!
- Certainly. I waffle over naming variables all the time and am happy to take other people's suggestions. Somewhat related to a question from @username_1 we could question why I even made this timeout configurable. It did not expect anyone to set it to 0 (although I did try that just to see the main loop peg one of the CPUs on my dev box), but, I suppose I could image a case where you had a box with a lot of CPUs and were willing to have one spin faster to minimize latency. The real reason I made in configurable was so it could play with it during testing without rebuilding my application.
- Regarding your questions: 1) I agree the timeout should never be set to 0. Not sure it should even be configurable. I did so really for testing purposes (so I could modify it without rebuilding my application). I suppose someone might want to tweak it to trade CPU for latency, but, I would be OK with not even making it configurable. The 10 ms value I based it on was not. 2) I do like the idea of having only one check. Originally I thought that the blockIfNoWork needed to come before the runTasks call, but, that was most likely before I found some race conditions and decided to add the (admittedly somewhat ugly) runLoopResumedSinceLastChecked boolean. Now I think it could be after and therefore the two checks could be combined. That will require a bit of testing (and thought). One other option I originally considered, but, dismissed as a bit risky was to remove the blockIfBusy check. The idea being that eventually if all the task were busy the Chooser would stop finding work and the new check would force a pause. I could not convince myself I understood the code well enough to guarantee that in all cases.

- @username_0 : I think you might misunderstood my first question. Now we have two waits here: one for the poll (task.poll.interval.ms), and the other for no work (task.max.no.work.wait.ms). My question is that since we can now use the second wait to control the polling (if there is no work, don't poll until task.max.no.work.wait.ms), seems we don't need the first wait anymore (equal to set task.poll.interval.ms=0). The AsyncRunLoop was relying on the first poll timer to avoid busy looping, but now it should be fine to return immediately after polling any SystemConsumer. This seems to be the goal we want to achieve here: AsyncRunLoop will control the polling by knowing whether there is worker available to process the message. And this should be much more efficient as you experiments demonstrated. What do you think?
- You are correct. I completely misread your first question. Without looking at the code I mistook it for a question I already had in my mind and went off into the weeds. Let me try again. I did not set the task.poll.interval.ms to 0 (which is used to set "pollIntervalMs"). I left it at its default 50 ms. I think it is still necessary to ensure that if some partitions have exhausted the their "unprocessedMessagesBySSP", but, others are keeping up with main loop Chooser (so that it always finds new work to process) that the main loop will still occasionally (every 50 ms) check to see if the currently empty partitions have new messages to "drain" from the bufferedMessages queue. This call should not block if the "timeout" variable is set to zero (when it is 0 this "poll" is really just a "drainTo"). My proposed update includes logic to ensure that timeout value is always set to 0 if we are not planning to update the Chooser during the call to choose (i.e., in the AsyncRunLoop case). I think this same logic stops the blocking/polling both in the "no work" case and in the "long time (50 ms) since last poll" case. On a related note when I first started working on this issue I thought the problem might be in the BlockingEnvelopeMap.poll method. I noted that it would block on the first SSP that did not have any messages (if the timeout was greater than zero) even if other empty partitions had messages ready to "drain". I reorganized the logic so it first "drained" all the queues and only then if it could not find at least one message to process start "polling" the SSPs one by one (and most likely blocking on the first one). That did not address my issue so I did not include that logic in my change.

I think the code will work in either location so if you prefer the previous order better (choose/run/block-delay) let me know.

Summary:
Allow other ways to use confluence.cluster.interface on Windows

Description:
h3. Summary +As a+ system admin on Windows +I want to+ be able to set network interface parameter {{confluence.cluster.interface}} on a fixed way +So that I can+ not use the name generated by Java and use one that is fixed on Windows instead h3. Problem Definition Customers report that the network interface name (for example, _eth0_) changes by itself on Windows, sometimes, on reboot. That is not a consistent behavior and cannot be reproduced. In this case, it changed form _eth6_ to _eth7_ and caused Synchrony to fail due to Hazelcast not finding it: {code} Hazelcast CANNOT start on this node. No matching network interface found.\nInterface matching must be either disabled or updated in the hazelcast.xml config file. {code} More information: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58632235/get-name-of-a-specific-network-interface-in-java http://hg.openjdk.java.net/jdk8/jdk8/jdk/file/82b276590b85/src/windows/native/java/net/NetworkInterface.c#l172 {quote} * Windows does not have any standard for device names so we are forced * to use our own convention which is based on the normal Unix naming * convention ("lo" for the loopback, eth0, eth1, .. for ethernet devices, * tr0, tr1, .. for token ring, and so on). This convention gives us * consistency across multiple Windows editions and also consistency with * Solaris/Linux device names. Note that we always enumerate in index * order and this ensures consistent device number across invocations. */ {quote} h3. Workaround Use the instruction on this kb, whenever that behavior is observed: [Hazelcast CANNOT start on this node. Title:
When the Mac is off the network and password expires

Description:
I have a question on how to prevent the password on the client from expiring and changing unless communication with the AD server is active, if it is needed. We can see ourselves in a position where on a remote client( working from home mac) the VPN connection software is broken. Active VPN needed to communicate to AD server for Laps. The LAPS password on the client has expired and changed and we have no way of finding it out. So we can't authenticate and re install/remove/fix the VPN software for the user. How does your Laps for mac make provision for this type of occurrence. Thanks

Comments:
- Hello @username_0! macOSLAPS when used with AD will not run unless it is able to contact Active Directory. If a user is at home and not connected to VPN you should see a log entry like this in `/Library/Logs/macOSLAPS.log`: ```Error|2022-03-20 08:57:36|macOSLAPS|Active Directory Node not available. Make sure your Active Directory is reachable via direct network connection or VPN.``` Let me know if that's helpful.

Title:
Fix for mobile wallet discovery + "memorynet"

Description:
<!--- Provide a general summary of your changes in the Title above --> ## Description <!--- Describe your changes in detail --> The DHT did not propagate private discovery messages to wallets because they do not have the `MESSAGE_PROPAGATION` feature. This PR changes the behaviour of the DHT to include wallets in discovery propagation messages. Internally, the Forward step of the DHT pipeline has a special case that will propagate to wallets. The closest peer selection has been adjusted to allow the caller to specify the PeerFeatures of the closest nodes to target by using the `neighbours_with_features` call. _NOTE:_ because those nodes will not propagate the message further, the selection ensures that a minimum number of propagation nodes are always selected This PR also includes a new example called "memorynet". `memorynet`, as the name suggests, is a small in-memory DHT network consisting of a number of "base nodes" and "wallets" (all that differs is their feature flags). The following happens when running `memorynet`: 1. A single "seed node", `NUM_NODES` "base nodes" and `NUM_WALLETS` "wallets" are generated and started. 1. All "base nodes" join the network via the "seed node" 1. All "wallets" join the network via a random "base node" 1. The first "wallet" in the list attempts to discover the last "wallet" in the list 1. The result of the discovery is printed and the network is shut down The example can be run with this command: `RUST_BACKTRACE=1 RUST_LOG=trace cargo run --example memorynet 2> /tmp/debug.log` ## Motivation and Context <!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? --> <!--- If it fixes an open issue, please link to the issue here. --> Closes #1204 The _memorynet_ example provides clean and easy to read output that allows you to easily see what is happening between a network of nodes. Each generated node is assigned a name that is used in stdout output.
